title: The carbocation: a flat + carbon and its empty p orbital
intent: After this scene the learner can say: "The + carbon of a carbocation has three bonds in one flat plane and six electrons. Its empty p orbital stands above and below that plane, and a lone pair of Cl⁻ flows into it to make the new bond."

products.name: chloroethane
products.note: C2 carries two H, so either face gives the same molecule.

beats.caption: CH₃CH₂⁺ seen edge-on. The + carbon has three bonds in one flat plane and only six electrons.
beats.captionOrbitals: The empty p orbital: one lobe above the flat + carbon, one below, and no electrons in it.

beats.caption: Cl⁻ comes in over the top face. One of its four lone pairs points straight at the empty lobe.

arrows.why: Lone pair → atom: a Cl⁻ pair (rich) fills the empty p orbital of the + carbon (poor) and becomes the C–Cl bond.

beats.caption: The lone pair flows into the empty p orbital and becomes the C–Cl bond: chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl.

stereoCallout.title: Flat cation, two faces
stereoCallout.text: The + carbon is flat, so Cl⁻ could come in over the top face or under the bottom one. Here C2 ends with two H, so both faces give the same chloroethane.

quiz.q: Why can Cl⁻ bond to the + carbon?

options.text: The + carbon has only six electrons and an empty p orbital, so it can take a pair.
options.why: Yes. Three bonds give six electrons; the empty p orbital is the room a lone pair of Cl⁻ fills.

options.text: The + carbon has a lone pair that it gives to Cl⁻.
options.why: The + carbon has no lone pair at all: three bonds and nothing else. The pair comes from Cl⁻.

options.text: Cl⁻ pulls a bond off the carbon to make room.
options.why: No bond breaks here. The carbon already has room: its empty p orbital. Cl⁻ simply gives it a pair.

notes: Added 2026-10-20 (novice review #3): Lesson 08 s15 explains the flat carbocation and its empty p orbital; this short primer shows exactly that, then step 2 of HCl + ethylene. The full HCl scene (17) stays on s13 and s17.
Course level: the cation is explained by electron counting and the empty p orbital; no hyperconjugation. A short primer: 3 beats, 14 s (the 25-50 s rule is for the reagent scenes).
